Building AI Voice Studio

A Complete Python & wxPython Guide
From Zero to Desktop Application

This book teaches you every concept of Python — basic, intermediate, and advanced — through the lens of a real-world desktop application: AI Voice Studio, a text-to-speech studio built with wxPython, sherpa-onnx, and NumPy.

By the time you finish, you will be able to build, test, and package a complete Python desktop application on your own.

First Edition • 2026 • Python 3.13 • wxPython 4.3
Based on AI Voice Studio (AIVS) open-source project

Preface

Who This Book Is For

This book is designed for programmers who want to learn Python from the ground up and apply their knowledge to build a real, functional desktop application. Whether you are a complete beginner, an intermediate developer expanding your skills, or an experienced programmer new to Python, this book provides a structured path from fundamentals to advanced topics.

How This Book Is Organized

The book is divided into eight parts:

  1. Part I — Python Fundamentals (Chapters 1–10): Variables, control flow, functions, file I/O, error handling, modules, and object-oriented basics.
  2. Part II — Intermediate Python (Chapters 11–18): Advanced OOP, decorators, context managers, regular expressions, testing, and structured data.
  3. Part III — Advanced Python (Chapters 19–26): Concurrency, multiprocessing, async I/O, type hints, metaclasses, design patterns, and introspection.
  4. Part IV — wxPython GUI Development (Chapters 27–36): Building desktop interfaces, event handling, threading in GUI apps, accessibility, and theming.
  5. Part V — Dependencies Deep Dive (Chapters 37–42): NumPy, Requests, sherpa-onnx, PDF/DOCX parsing, FFmpeg, and virtual environments.
  6. Part VI — Building AI Voice Studio (Chapters 43–60): The complete project from architecture to every major subsystem.
  7. Part VII — Testing & Deployment (Chapters 61–66): Unit testing, mocking, PyInstaller, Inno Setup, and CI/CD.
  8. Part VIII — Advanced Topics (Chapters 67–72): Managed runtime, subprocess architecture, logging, performance, and security.

The Running Example: AI Voice Studio

Rather than teaching concepts in isolation, every chapter applies what it teaches to AI Voice Studio (AIVS) — a production-quality desktop application that converts text documents into spoken audio using neural TTS engines. The project demonstrates:

  • wxPython GUI with accessibility support (NVDA, JAWS, Narrator)
  • Multiple TTS engines (Piper, Kokoro, Matcha, Kitten, XTTS v2 cloning)
  • Document parsing (PDF, DOCX, HTML, Markdown, EPUB)
  • Background threading for non-blocking synthesis
  • Virtual environment management and addon architecture
  • PyInstaller packaging and Inno Setup installers
  • 99+ unit tests with comprehensive coverage

Prerequisites

  • A computer running Windows (primary), macOS, or Linux
  • Python 3.11 or later installed
  • A text editor or IDE (VS Code, PyCharm, or similar)
  • No prior Python experience required — we start from scratch

How to Use This Book

Each chapter follows a consistent structure:

SectionPurpose
Learning ObjectivesWhat you will master in this chapter
Core ConceptsThorough explanation with syntax and semantics
Code ExamplesWorking examples with output, drawn from the AIVS project
AIVS in ActionHow the concept appears in the real project
ExercisesPractice problems to reinforce learning
Key TakeawaysSummary of the most important points
Interactive Learning: Every code example in this book can be typed into a Python REPL or saved to a .py file and executed. The AI Voice Studio project files are referenced by their actual paths in the repository.

Ch01 Introduction
Chapter 1

Introduction & Setup

Learning Objectives

  • Understand what Python is and why it dominates desktop and AI development
  • Install Python 3.13 on Windows, macOS, or Linux
  • Set up a command-line terminal and run your first Python program
  • Explore the AI Voice Studio project structure
  • Create and activate a virtual environment
  • Install project dependencies

1.1 What Is Python?

Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. It emphasizes code readability with its use of significant indentation and English-like syntax. Today, Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world, powering everything from web servers to artificial intelligence to desktop applications.

Why Python?

FeatureBenefit
InterpretedNo compilation step — run code immediately
Dynamically typedNo type declarations needed (but available via hints)
Extensive stdlibOver 200 modules in the standard library
Massive ecosystem400,000+ packages on PyPI
Cross-platformWindows, macOS, Linux with one codebase
AI/ML dominanceNumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow all use Python
Desktop GUIswxPython, PyQt, Tkinter, Kivy

Python in AI Voice Studio

AI Voice Studio is a desktop application that converts text documents into spoken audio using neural text-to-speech (TTS) engines. It is built entirely in Python with wxPython for the GUI. This makes it a perfect learning vehicle because it touches every major area of Python development:

  • Core Python: File I/O, string processing, data structures, error handling
  • OOP: Classes, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation
  • Concurrency: Threading for background TTS synthesis
  • GUI: wxPython for native Windows interface
  • AI/ML: sherpa-onnx for neural speech synthesis
  • Networking: HTTP downloads of voice models
  • Packaging: PyInstaller and Inno Setup for distribution

1.2 Installing Python

System Requirements

  • Operating System: Windows 10/11 (64-bit), macOS 12+, or Ubuntu 20.04+
  • Python version: 3.11 or later (we use 3.13)
  • RAM: 4 GB minimum, 8 GB recommended
  • Disk: 2 GB free space (for TTS voice models)

Windows Installation

  1. Visit python.org/downloads
  2. Download the Windows installer (64-bit)
  3. Run the installer. Important: Check the box that says "Add python.exe to PATH" before clicking Install
  4. Verify the installation by opening a terminal and typing: 
    python --version
# Output: Python 3.13.0

    Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 1)

    1. Line 1: python --version
      python --version
    2. Line 2: # Output: Python 3.13.0
      A comment: Output: Python 3.13.0.
Always add Python to PATH during installation. If you skip this, you will not be able to run python or pip from the terminal without specifying the full path.

macOS / Linux Installation

# macOS (using Homebrew)
brew install python@3.13

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3.13 python3.13-venv python3.13-dev

# Verify
python3 --version

What Each Module Does

ModulePurposeKey Concepts
main.py Entry point: creates wx.App, shows MainFrame Script execution, if __name__
constants.py All magic numbers and string constants Module-level constants, enums
paths.py Cross-platform path management os.path, pathlib
settings.py JSON-based user preferences File I/O, JSON, defaults
project.py Project persistence (save/load) JSON, atomic writes
gui/main_frame.py Main application window wxPython frames, menus, events
tts/engine.py Sherpa-onnx TTS wrapper CTypes, audio processing
jobs/synthesizer.py Background TTS processing Threading, events, callbacks
addons/__init__.py Plugin/addon system Dynamic imports, JSON manifests
python_runtime/__init__.py Managed virtual environment Subprocess, venv creation

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

A virtual environment is an isolated Python environment that prevents dependency conflicts between projects. This is one of the most important practices in Python development: 

# Create a virtual environment named .venv
python -m venv .venv

# Activate it (Windows PowerShell)
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

# Activate it (Windows Command Prompt)
.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

# Activate it (macOS/Linux)
source .venv/bin/activate

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 8)

  1. Line 1: # Create a virtual environment named .venv
    A comment: Create a virtual environment named .venv.
  2. Line 2: python -m venv .venv
    python -m venv .venv
  3. Line 3: # Activate it (Windows PowerShell)
    A comment: Activate it (Windows PowerShell).
  4. Line 4: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
    .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
  5. Line 5: # Activate it (Windows Command Prompt)
    A comment: Activate it (Windows Command Prompt).

  7. Line 7: # Activate it (macOS/Linux)

  8. Line 8: source .venv/bin/activate
    source .venv/bin/activate

Once activated, your terminal prompt changes to show (.venv), and all Python/pip commands use the isolated environment: 

(.venv) $ python --version
Python 3.13.0
(.venv) $ pip --version
pip 24.2 from .venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/pip

Step 3: Install Dependencies

AI Voice Studio requires six core dependencies:

# Install from requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 10)

  1. Line 1: # Install from requirements.txt
    A comment: Install from requirements.txt.
  2. Line 2: pip install -r requirements.txt
    pip install -r requirements.txt
PackageVersionPurpose
wxPython ≥4.3.1 Cross-platform native GUI toolkit
sherpa-onnx ≥1.13.0 Neural TTS engine (ONNX runtime)
numpy ≥2.0 Numerical array operations for audio
requests ≥2.31 HTTP client for downloading models
pypdf ≥5.0 PDF document parsing
python-docx ≥1.1 Word document (.docx) parsing
Why virtual environments? Without them, installing wxPython for one project could overwrite packages needed by another. The .venv directory contains a complete, isolated Python installation. It is listed in .gitignore so it is never committed to version control.

1.7 A Note on Python Versions

This book targets Python 3.13, but all code is compatible with Python 3.11+. Here are the key version features we use:

VersionFeatureExample
3.6+ f-strings f"Hello {name}"
3.7+ dataclasses @dataclass class Foo:
3.8+ Walrus operator := if (n := len(x)) > 5:
3.9+ Built-in generics list[str] instead of List[str]
3.10+ match/case match command: case "quit":
3.11+ Exception groups except* ValueError:
3.12+ Type parameter syntax def foo[T](x: T) -> T:

1.8 IDE Setup

While any text editor works, a proper IDE dramatically improves productivity.

VS Code (Recommended)

  1. Install VS Code
  2. Install the Python extension by Microsoft
  3. Install the Pylance extension for type checking
  4. Open the project folder and select the .venv as the interpreter

PyCharm

  1. Install PyCharm (Community is free)
  2. Open the project directory
  3. Go to Settings → Project → Python Interpreter → Add → Existing Environment → select .venv/Scripts/python.exe

1.9 The GitHub Copilot / AI-Assisted Development

Modern Python development often includes AI assistants. Throughout this book, we write code that is readable and well-documented — exactly the kind of code that AI assistants work best with. The AI Voice Studio project itself follows these principles:

  • Clear variable and function names (no single-letter variables except loop counters)
  • Docstrings on every public class and function
  • Type hints on function signatures
  • Constants instead of magic numbers

1.10 Key Takeaways

  • Python is interpreted — you write code and run it directly, no compilation step needed
  • Virtual environments are essential for isolating project dependencies
  • AI Voice Studio is a production-quality Python desktop app that demonstrates every major Python concept
  • The project has 53 Python source files across 13 subpackages, plus 12 test files
  • All core dependencies (wxPython, sherpa-onnx, numpy, requests, pypdf, python-docx) are installed from requirements.txt
  • The test suite has 99+ tests — good testing is not optional in real projects
  • An IDE with Python support makes development much more productive

Chapter 2

Variables & Data Types

Learning Objectives

  • Understand Python's dynamic typing system
  • Master all primitive data types: int, float, bool, str, None
  • Learn variable naming conventions and best practices
  • Understand type checking and type conversion
  • See how AI Voice Studio uses variables and constants

2.1 Python Is Dynamically Typed

Unlike languages such as C, Java, or Go, Python does not require you to declare the type of a variable. The type is determined at runtime based on the value assigned: 

# Python figures out the type automatically
name = "AI Voice Studio"      # str
version = 2.0                  # float
year = 2026                     # int
is_released = True              # bool
nothing = None                  # NoneType

# You can reassign to a different type (though you usually shouldn't)
x = 42       # int
x = "hello"  # now str — Python doesn't care

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 1)

  1. Line 1: # Python figures out the type automatically
    A comment: Python figures out the type automatically.
  2. Line 2: name = "AI Voice Studio" # str
    Assigns "AI Voice Studio" # str to name.
  3. Line 3: version = 2.0 # float
    Assigns 2.0 # float to version.
  4. Line 4: year = 2026 # int
  5. Line 5: is_released = True # bool
    Assigns True # bool to is_released.
  6. Line 6: nothing = None # NoneType
    Assigns None # NoneType to nothing.
  7. Line 7: # You can reassign to a different type (though you usually shouldn't)
    A comment: You can reassign to a different type (though you usually shouldn't).
  8. Line 8: x = 42 # int
    Assigns 42 # int to x.
  9. Line 9: x = "hello" # now str — Python doesn't care
    Assigns "hello" # now str — Python doesn't care to x.

This flexibility makes Python fast to write but requires discipline. The project uses type hints (Chapter 22) to document expected types without enforcing them at runtime.

The type() Function

Use type() to check a variable's type at any time:

>>> type(42)
<class 'int'>
>>> type(3.14)
<class 'float'>
>>> type("hello")
<class 'str'>
>>> type(True)
<class 'bool'>
>>> type(None)
<class 'NoneType'>

The isinstance() Function

More Pythonic than type() == SomeType is using isinstance(), which also works with inheritance: 

x = 42
print(isinstance(x, int))        # True
print(isinstance(x, (int, float))) # True — can check multiple types

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 3)

  1. Line 1: x = 42
    Assigns 42 to x.
  2. Line 2: print(isinstance(x, int)) # True
    Checks if an object is an instance of a class. Preferred over type() for type checking.
  3. Line 3: print(isinstance(x, (int, float))) # True — can check multiple types
    Checks if an object is an instance of a class. Preferred over type() for type checking.

2.2 Numeric Types

Integers (int)

Python integers have arbitrary precision — they can be as large as your memory allows. No overflow: 

# Normal integers
segments = 42
sample_rate = 24000

# Very large integers (no overflow!)
huge = 10 ** 100  # a googol

# Different bases
binary = 0b1010    # = 10 in decimal
octal = 0o17       # = 15 in decimal
hexadecimal = 0xFF  # = 255 in decimal

# Underscores for readability (Python 3.6+)
max_concurrent = 1_000_000  # same as 1000000

Floats (float)

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)  # False!

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))  # True

Float comparison is a classic Python gotcha. Never use == to compare floats for equality. Instead, check if they are close enough: abs(a - b) < 1e-9 or use math.isclose(a, b).

2.3 Booleans

bool is a subclass of int — True is 1, False is 0: 

is_running = True
has_gpu = False

# Booleans participate in arithmetic
print(True + True + False)  # 2
print(True * 10)              # 10

# Truthiness: many values are "truthy" or "falsy"
print(bool(1))        # True
print(bool(0))        # False
print(bool("hello"))  # True (non-empty string)
print(bool(""))       # False (empty string)
print(bool([]))       # False (empty list)
print(bool([1]))     # True (non-empty list)
print(bool(None))     # False

Boolean Operators

# and, or, not
has_gpu = True
runtime_installed = False

use_cpu = not has_gpu or runtime_installed   # False

# Short-circuit evaluation (important for performance)
# "and" stops at the first False, "or" stops at the first True
result = False and expensive_function()  # expensive_function() never called!

2.4 Strings

Strings in Python are immutable sequences of Unicode characters. They are one of the most commonly used types: 

# String creation (three ways)
name = "AI Voice Studio"       # double quotes
name = 'AI Voice Studio'       # single quotes (same thing)
doc = """This is a
multi-line string."""         # triple quotes

# Strings are immutable
s = "hello"
# s[0] = "H"  # TypeError! Can't change characters

# Must create a new string
s = "H" + s[1:]   # "Hello"

  3. Line 3: name = 'AI Voice Studio' # single quotes (same thing)
    Assigns 'AI Voice Studio' # single quotes (same thing) to name.
  4. Line 4: doc = """This is a
    Assigns """This is a to doc.
  5. Line 5: multi-line string.""" # triple quotes
    multi-line string.""" # triple quotes
  6. Line 6: # Strings are immutable
    A comment: Strings are immutable.
  7. Line 7: s = "hello"
    Assigns "hello" to s.
  8. Line 8: # s[0] = "H" # TypeError! Can't change characters

Common String Operations

text = "Hello, AI Voice Studio!"

# Length
print(len(text))            # 23

# Indexing (0-based)
print(text[0])              # "H"
print(text[-1])             # "!" (last character)

# Slicing [start:stop:step]
print(text[7:19])           # "AI Voice Stud"
print(text[::2])             # "HloAVcsad!" (every other char)

# Methods
print(text.upper())          # "HELLO, AI VOICE STUDIO!"
print(text.lower())          # "hello, ai voice studio!"
print(text.replace("AI", "ML"))  # "Hello, ML Voice Studio!"
print(text.split(", "))       # ["Hello", "AI Voice Studio!"]
print(text.find("Voice"))     # 7 (index of first match)
print(text.startswith("Hello"))  # True
print(text.endswith("!"))      # True

# Stripping whitespace
padded = "  hello  "
print(padded.strip())        # "hello"
print(padded.lstrip())       # "hello  "

  11. Line 11: print(text.upper()) # "HELLO, AI VOICE STUDIO!"

  12. Line 12: print(text.lower()) # "hello, ai voice studio!"

String Formatting (f-strings)

F-strings (Python 3.6+) are the preferred way to embed expressions in strings:

name = "Piper"
voices = 153

# Basic interpolation
print(f"TTS engine: {name}")

# Expressions inside braces
print(f"{name.upper()} has {voices * 2} total voice files")

# Format specifiers
pi = 3.14159
print(f"Pi to 2 decimal places: {pi:.2f}")   # 3.14
print(f"Right-aligned: '{42:10}'")         # '        42'
print(f"Zero-padded: {42:05d}")             # 00042
print(f"Percentage: {0.857:.1%}")          # 85.7%
print(f"Bytes: {1048576:,.0f}")             # 1,048,576

# Debugging: = shows expression AND result
voices = 153
print(f"{voices = }")                      # voices = 153

Strings in AI Voice Studio

String processing is central to text-to-speech. Here are real examples from the project:

# From ai_voice_studio/util.py
import re

def sanitize_filename(name: str, max_length: int = 80) -> str:
    """Remove or replace characters that are unsafe in filenames."""
    # Replace characters illegal on Windows
    name = re.sub(r'[<>:"/\\|?*]', '_', name)
    # Collapse whitespace
    name = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', name).strip()
    # Truncate to max length
    if len(name) > max_length:
        name = name[:max_length].rstrip()
    return name

# Usage:
safe = sanitize_filename("My Book: Chapter 1? Yes!")
print(safe)  # "My Book_ Chapter 1_ Yes!"

    Docstring: Remove or replace characters that are unsafe in filenames.. Documents the purpose of the following code.
  5. Line 5: # Replace characters illegal on Windows
    A comment: Replace characters illegal on Windows.

    Replaces all matches with the replacement string.
  7. Line 7: # Collapse whitespace

2.5 The None Type

None is Python's way of representing "nothing" or "no value." It is a singleton — there is exactly one None object in the entire Python runtime: 

result = None

# Always compare with "is", not "=="
if result is None:
    print("No result yet")

# ⚠️ Wrong:
if result == None:  # Works but un-Pythonic; can be overridden
    pass

# None has a falsy boolean value
print(bool(None))  # False

  1. Line 1: result = None
    Assigns None to result.
  2. Line 2: # Always compare with "is", not "=="
    A comment: Always compare with "is", not "==".
  3. Line 3: if result is None:
    Checks condition: result is None. The indented block runs only when this is True.
  4. Line 4: print("No result yet")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  5. Line 5: # ⚠️ Wrong:
    A comment: ⚠️ Wrong:.
  6. Line 6: if result == None: # Works but un-Pythonic; can be overridden
    Checks condition: result == None. The indented block runs only when this is True.
  7. Line 7: pass
    Placeholder: does nothing.
  8. Line 8: # None has a falsy boolean value
    A comment: None has a falsy boolean value.

In AI Voice Studio, None is used extensively for "not set" values:

# From ai_voice_studio/clone/__init__.py
class CloneClient:
    def __init__(self, timeout: float = 600.0):
        self._proc: subprocess.Popen | None = None  # No process yet

    def _ensure_proc(self):
        if self._proc is not None and self._proc.poll() is None:
            return  # Process already running
        # ... start new process

2.7 Type Conversion (Casting)

Python does not automatically convert between types, but you can do it explicitly:

# int → float
x = float(42)     # 42.0

# float → int (truncates toward zero)
x = int(3.9)      # 3 (NOT 4!)
x = int(-3.9)     # -3

# int/float → str
s = str(42)       # "42"
s = str(3.14)     # "3.14"

# str → int
n = int("42")     # 42
# int("hello")  # ValueError!

# str → float
f = float("3.14") # 3.14

# int → bool
print(bool(0))    # False
print(bool(1))    # True
print(bool(42))   # True (any non-zero is True)

2.8 Mutable vs. Immutable

This distinction is crucial in Python. Immutable objects cannot be changed after creation; mutable objects can:

ImmutableMutable
int, float, complexlist
strdict
tupleset
frozensetbytearray
bytesObjects (instances of classes)
NoneType
 
# Immutable: assignment creates a new object
a = "hello"
b = a          # b points to the SAME string
a = "world"   # Now a points to a NEW string
print(b)       # "hello" — b is unchanged!

# Mutable: assignment creates a reference
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a          # b points to the SAME list
a.append(4)    # Modifies the shared list
print(b)       # [1, 2, 3, 4] — b is also changed!

# To make an independent copy:
b = a.copy()   # or b = list(a) or b = a[:]

    Assigns a # b points to the SAME string to b.

The project stores settings as a mutable dict. When saving, it serializes the entire dict to JSON. This "snapshot" approach means the settings are effectively immutable at the file level, even though the in-memory dict is mutable.

2.9 Identity vs. Equality

Python has two ways to compare objects:

# == checks VALUE equality
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == b)    # True — same contents

# "is" checks IDENTITY (same object in memory)
print(a is b)    # False — different list objects

# For singletons like None, always use "is"
x = None
print(x is None)    # True ✓
print(x == None)    # Also True, but un-Pythonic ✗

# Small integers are cached (CPython optimization)
a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)    # True — both refer to cached object

a = 257
b = 257
print(a is b)    # False (usually) — outside the cache range

2.10 Augmented Assignment

Shorthand operators that modify and assign in one step:

x = 10
x += 5    # x = x + 5  → 15
x -= 3    # x = x - 3  → 12
x *= 2    # x = x * 2  → 24
x /= 4    # x = x / 4  → 6.0 (note: always float after /)
x //= 2   # x = x // 2 → 3.0 (floor division)
x %= 2    # x = x % 2  → 1.0 (modulo)

# For strings, += creates a new string
msg = "Hello"
msg += ", World!"  # "Hello, World!"

# For lists, += extends in-place (mutates)
items = [1, 2]
items += [3, 4]  # items is now [1, 2, 3, 4]

2.11 Unpacking

Python's unpacking syntax makes assignments clean and readable:

# Tuple unpacking
x, y, z = 1, 2, 3

# Swap variables (no temp variable needed!)
a, b = 10, 20
a, b = b, a  # a=20, b=10

# Star unpacking (Python 3+)
first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# first=1, middle=[2,3,4], last=5

# Ignoring values with _
name, _, version = "Piper", "en_US", "medium"

# Dict unpacking (Python 3.5+)
defaults = {"rate": 1.0, "pitch": 1.0, "volume": 1.0}
overrides = {"rate": 1.5}
params = {**defaults, **overrides}  # {"rate": 1.5, "pitch": 1.0, "volume": 1.0}

2.13 Variables in the AIVS Constants Module

The AI Voice Studio project centralizes all magic numbers and strings in constants.py. This is a best practice for larger projects:

Why constants? If you use the string "wav" in 15 different files and later decide to rename it, you would have to find and replace in all 15 files. With a constant, you change it in one place. Constants also serve as documentation — FORMAT_WAV tells you what the value means at a glance.

2.14 Key Takeaways

  • Python is dynamically typed — variables have no declared type, but every value has a type
  • Five core types: int, float, bool, str, None
  • Integers have arbitrary precision — no overflow
  • Floats have limited precision — never use == for comparison
  • Strings are immutable — operations create new strings
  • Use is for None comparison, == for value equality
  • Constants go in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE and live in a dedicated module
  • Type hints document expected types without enforcing them
  • F-strings are the modern way to format strings

Exercise 2.3: Look at the constants.py file in the project. How many constant values are defined? Pick three and explain what they control in the application.

Ch03 Control Flow
Chapter 3

Control Flow

Learning Objectives

  • Master if, elif, else branching
  • Use for and while loops effectively
  • Understand break, continue, and else on loops
  • Apply the Python 3.10+ match/case statement
  • See control flow patterns in AI Voice Studio

3.1 if / elif / else

The if statement executes code based on a boolean condition:

# Basic if
has_gpu = True
if has_gpu:
    print("Using CUDA GPU")

# if / else
compute = "cpu"
if compute == "cuda":
    print("GPU mode")
else:
    print("CPU mode")

# if / elif / else (chain multiple conditions)
quality = "medium"
if quality == "low":
    size_mb = 50
elif quality == "medium":
    size_mb = 200
elif quality == "high":
    size_mb = 500
else:
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown quality: {quality}")

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 1)

  1. Line 1: # Basic if
    A comment: Basic if.
  2. Line 2: has_gpu = True
    Assigns True to has_gpu.
  3. Line 3: if has_gpu:
    Checks condition: has_gpu. The indented block runs only when this is True.
  4. Line 4: print("Using CUDA GPU")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  5. Line 5: # if / else
    A comment: if / else.
  6. Line 6: compute = "cpu"
    Assigns "cpu" to compute.
  7. Line 7: if compute == "cuda":
    Checks condition: compute == "cuda". The indented block runs only when this is True.
  8. Line 8: print("GPU mode")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  9. Line 9: else:
    Fallback: executes when none of the above conditions matched.
  10. Line 10: print("CPU mode")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  11. Line 11: # if / elif / else (chain multiple conditions)
    A comment: if / elif / else (chain multiple conditions).
  12. Line 12: quality = "medium"
    Assigns "medium" to quality.
  13. Line 13: if quality == "low":
    Checks condition: quality == "low". The indented block runs only when this is True.
  14. Line 14: size_mb = 50
    Assigns 50 to size_mb.
  15. Line 15: elif quality == "medium":
    Alternative condition: quality == "medium". Checked only if all previous conditions were False.
  16. Line 16: size_mb = 200
    Assigns 200 to size_mb.
  17. Line 17: elif quality == "high":
    Alternative condition: quality == "high". Checked only if all previous conditions were False.
  18. Line 18: size_mb = 500
    Assigns 500 to size_mb.
  19. Line 19: else:
    Fallback: executes when none of the above conditions matched.
  20. Line 20: raise ValueError(f"Unknown quality: {quality}")
    Raised when a function receives an argument of the right type but inappropriate value.

Important: No Parentheses or Braces

# Python style — NO parentheses around conditions
if x > 5:          # ✓ Correct
    pass

# if (x > 5):      # ✗ Works but un-Pythonic
#     pass

# Indentation defines the block (4 spaces standard)
if True:
    print("line 1")
    print("line 2")  # Still inside the if
print("line 3")     # Outside the if

3.2 for Loops

Python's for loop iterates over any iterable — lists, strings, tuples, dicts, sets, ranges, files, generators, and more: 

# Iterate over a list
engines = ["Piper", "Kokoro", "Matcha"]
for engine in engines:
    print(f"Loading {engine}...")

# Iterate over a string
for char in "hello":
    print(char, end=" ")  # h e l l o

# range() — generate number sequences
for i in range(5):        # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
    print(i)

for i in range(2, 10, 3): # start, stop, step: 2, 5, 8
    print(i)

# Iterate with index using enumerate()
for idx, engine in enumerate(engines):
    print(f"{idx}: {engine}")
# 0: Piper
# 1: Kokoro
# 2: Matcha

            for voice in variant.get("voices", []):

                    "tts": tts["id"],
                    "language": lang["code"],
                    "voice": voice["id"],
                    "sid": voice.get("sid", 0),

3.3 while Loops

while loops repeat as long as a condition is true:

# Basic while loop
countdown = 5
while countdown > 0:
    print(f"{countdown}...")
    countdown -= 1
print("Go!")

# Reading input until a sentinel value
while True:
    line = input("Enter command (or 'quit'): ")
    if line == "quit":
        break
    print(f"Executing: {line}")

# Polling pattern (used in AIVS server health checks)
import time
timeout = 30
deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
while time.monotonic() < deadline:
    if health_check():
        print("Server is ready!")
        break
    time.sleep(1.0)
else:
    print("Server did not start in time")

  3. Line 3: while countdown > 0:
    While loop: repeats as long as countdown > 0.
  4. Line 4: print(f"{countdown}...")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  5. Line 5: countdown -= 1
    Updates countdown by -= 1.
  6. Line 6: print("Go!")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  7. Line 7: # Reading input until a sentinel value
    A comment: Reading input until a sentinel value.

The while-else Pattern

When a while loop finishes normally (condition becomes false), the else block runs. If the loop exits via break, the else is skipped: 

# From omnivoice_server/__init__.py — health check polling
while time.monotonic() < deadline:
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=5) as resp:
            if resp.status == 200:
                self._ready.set()
                return  # Success — else block is skipped
    except (urllib.error.URLError, OSError):
        pass
    time.sleep(1.0)
raise OmniVoiceServerError(
    f"Server did not become ready within {timeout}
)

    Begins exception handling. Code in this block is monitored for errors.
  4. Line 4: with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=5) as resp:
    Opens a file and returns a file object. Supports modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write), 'a' (append), 'b' (binary).

3.4 break, continue, and pass

# break — exit the loop immediately
for engine in ["piper", "kokoro", "matcha"]:
    if engine_is_available(engine):
        chosen = engine
        break  # Stop searching once we find one
else:
    raise RuntimeError("No TTS engine available!")

# continue — skip to the next iteration
for voice in all_voices:
    if not voice.get("enabled", True):
        continue  # Skip disabled voices
    print(voice["name"])

# pass — do nothing (placeholder)
class NotImplementedEngine:
    pass  # Will implement later

3.5 List Comprehensions

List comprehensions are a concise way to create lists. They combine a loop and an expression into a single line: 

# Traditional loop
squares = []
for x in range(10):
    squares.append(x ** 2)

# List comprehension (equivalent, more Pythonic)
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]
# [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81]

# With filtering
even_squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
# [0, 4, 16, 36, 64]

# Dict comprehension
engine_names = {t["id"]: t["name"] for t in tts_list}
# {"piper": "Piper TTS", "kokoro": "Kokoro TTS", ...}

# Set comprehension
languages = {v["language"] for v in installed_voices}
# {"en", "zh", "ja", "multi", ...}

# Generator expression (lazy — doesn't create list in memory)
total = sum(len(v["text"]) for v in segments)

  1. Line 1: # Traditional loop
    A comment: Traditional loop.
  2. Line 2: squares = []
    Assigns [] to squares.
  3. Line 3: for x in range(10):
    Generates a sequence of integers. Commonly used in for loops.
  4. Line 4: squares.append(x ** 2)
    Adds a single item to the end of the list.
  5. Line 5: # List comprehension (equivalent, more Pythonic)
    A comment: List comprehension (equivalent, more Pythonic).

3.6 match/case (Python 3.10+)

Python 3.10 introduced match/case, similar to switch/case in other languages but much more powerful: 

# Basic match/case
command = "synthesize"

match command:
    case "ping":
        print("Pong!")
    case "synthesize":
        print("Generating audio...")
    case "quit":
        print("Goodbye!")
    case _:
        print(f"Unknown command: {command}")  # _ is wildcard

# Matching with capture variables
match request:
    case {"cmd": "synthesize", "text": text}:
        process_text(text)
    case {"cmd": "ping"}:
        respond_ok()
    case _:
        respond_error("Unknown command")

# Matching with guards (extra conditions)
match quality:
    case q if q < 50:
        print("Low quality")
    case q if q < 200:
        print("Medium quality")
    case _:
        print("High quality")

3.7 Nested Loops and Loop else

# Nested loops — common in catalog traversal
for tts in tts_list:
    for lang in tts.get("languages", []):
        for variant in lang.get("variants", []):
            if variant["id"] == target:
                print(f"Found: {tts['id']} / {lang['code']} / {target}")
                break
        else:
            continue  # Only reached if inner loop didn't break
        break  # Break outer loop too
    else:
        print("Not found")

  3. Line 3: for lang in tts.get("languages", []):
    Returns the value for a key, or a default value if the key doesn't exist. Safer than direct access.
  4. Line 4: for variant in lang.get("variants", []):
    Returns the value for a key, or a default value if the key doesn't exist. Safer than direct access.
  5. Line 5: if variant["id"] == target:
    Checks condition: variant["id"] == target. The indented block runs only when this is True.
  6. Line 6: print(f"Found: {tts['id']} / {lang['code']} / {target}")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  7. Line 7: break
    Exits the innermost loop.
  8. Line 8: else:
    Fallback: executes when none of the above conditions matched.
  9. Line 9: continue # Only reached if inner loop didn't break
    continue # Only reached if inner loop didn't break

For-Else Pattern

# The "else" after a for loop runs only if the loop completes without break
for file in candidates:
    if os.path.isfile(file):
        print(f"Using: {file}")
        break
else:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No suitable file found")

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 14)

  1. Line 1: # The "else" after a for loop runs only if the loop completes without break
    A comment: The "else" after a for loop runs only if the loop completes without break.
  2. Line 2: for file in candidates:
    Iterates over candidates, assigning each element to file.
  3. Line 3: if os.path.isfile(file):
    OS-agnostic path manipulation. Use join(), exists(), dirname(), basename(), splitext().
  4. Line 4: print(f"Using: {file}")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  5. Line 5: break
    Exits the innermost loop.
  6. Line 6: else:
    Fallback: executes when none of the above conditions matched.
  7. Line 7: raise FileNotFoundError("No suitable file found")
    Raised when a file or directory is requested but doesn't exist.

    for v in all_voices

3.9 Key Takeaways

  • Indentation defines blocks — use 4 spaces consistently
  • for iterates over any iterable; use enumerate() for index + value
  • while repeats while a condition is true
  • break exits the innermost loop; continue skips to next iteration
  • Loop else runs when the loop completes without break
  • List comprehensions are concise and often faster than equivalent loops
  • match/case (3.10+) is powerful for pattern matching on dicts and sequences
  • The AIVS catalog uses nested for loops to traverse TTS → language → variant → voice hierarchies

Ch04 Functions
Chapter 4

Functions

Learning Objectives

  • Define and call functions with parameters and return values
  • Master default arguments, *args, and **kwargs
  • Understand scope (LEGB rule) and closures
  • Use lambda functions for short throwaway operations
  • See function patterns used throughout AI Voice Studio

4.1 Defining Functions

# Basic function definition
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    """Return a greeting for the given name."""  # Docstring
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

# Call the function
message = greet("Developer")
print(message)  # Hello, Developer!

# Functions without a return statement return None implicitly
def log_event(event: str):
    print(f"[LOG] {event}")
    # No return → returns None

result = log_event("app started")
print(result)  # None

    Returns f"Hello, {name}!" to the caller.

    A comment: Call the function.

    Assigns greet("Developer") to message.

  8. Line 8: # Functions without a return statement return None implicitly
    A comment: Functions without a return statement return None implicitly.

Function Anatomy

ComponentPurpose

Never use mutable objects (lists, dicts) as default parameters! They are created once at function definition time and shared across all calls: 
# WRONG — shared mutable default!
def add_voice(voice, voices=[]):
    voices.append(voice)
    return voices

# RIGHT — create a new list each call
def add_voice(voice, voices=None):
    if voices is None:
        voices = []
    voices.append(voice)
    return voices

Arbitrary Arguments (*args and **kwargs)

# *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple
def log_all(*messages: str):
    for msg in messages:
        print(f"[LOG] {msg}")

log_all("Starting", "Loading models", "Ready")

# **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict
def create_engine(engine_id: str, **options):
    print(f"Engine: {engine_id}")
    for key, value in options.items():
        print(f"  {key} = {value}")

create_engine("piper", device="cpu", threads=4, verbose=True)
# Engine: piper
#   device = cpu
#   threads = 4
#   verbose = True

# Combining positional, keyword, *args, **kwargs
def configure(name: str, *engines, debug=False, **settings):
    pass

4.3 Return Values

# Single return value
def get_sample_rate(voice: dict) -> int:
    return voice.get("sample_rate", 24000)

# Multiple return values (returns a tuple)
def parse_voice_id(voice_id: str) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """Split 'en_US/medium' into (language, variant)."""
    parts = voice_id.split("/")
    return parts[0], parts[1]  # Implicit tuple packing

lang, variant = parse_voice_id("en_US/medium")  # Tuple unpacking

# Returning None for "not found"
def find_voice(voices: list, voice_id: str) -> dict | None:
    for v in voices:
        if v["id"] == voice_id:
            return v
    return None

4.4 Scope — The LEGB Rule

Python looks up variable names in this order: Local → Enclosing → Global → Built-in.

# Global scope
APP_NAME = "AI Voice Studio"

def outer():
    # Enclosing scope
    version = "2.0"

    def inner():
        # Local scope
        print(APP_NAME)    # Global — found
        print(version)     # Enclosing — found
        print(len("hi"))   # Built-in — found
        name = "inner"    # Local variable

    inner()

outer()

  1. Line 1: # Global scope
    A comment: Global scope.
  2. Line 2: APP_NAME = "AI Voice Studio"
    Assigns "AI Voice Studio" to APP_NAME.
  3. Line 3: def outer():
    Defines function outer.
  4. Line 4: # Enclosing scope
    A comment: Enclosing scope.
  5. Line 5: version = "2.0"
    Assigns "2.0" to version.
  6. Line 6: def inner():
    Defines function inner.
  7. Line 7: # Local scope
    A comment: Local scope.
  8. Line 8: print(APP_NAME) # Global — found
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  9. Line 9: print(version) # Enclosing — found
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  10. Line 10: print(len("hi")) # Built-in — found
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  11. Line 11: name = "inner" # Local variable
    Assigns "inner" # Local variable to name.
  12. Line 12: inner()
    Calls function inner().
  13. Line 13: outer()
    Calls function outer().

global and nonlocal

# global — modify a global variable from inside a function
counter = 0

def increment():
    global counter
    counter += 1

increment()
print(counter)  # 1

# nonlocal — modify an enclosing scope variable
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment

counter = make_counter()
print(counter())  # 1
print(counter())  # 2

4.5 Lambda Functions

Lambdas are anonymous, single-expression functions:

# Regular function
def double(x):
    return x * 2

# Equivalent lambda
double = lambda x: x * 2

# Common use cases

# Sorting with a key function
voices = [
    {"name": "Zoe", "sid": 5},
    {"name": "Adam", "sid": 1},
    {"name": "Bella", "sid": 3},
]
sorted_voices = sorted(voices, key=lambda v: v["sid"])

# Filtering
big_voices = list(filter(lambda v: v["sid"] > 3, voices))

# Mapping
names = list(map(lambda v: v["name"], voices))

# In AIVS — callback in thread setup
threading.Thread(
    target=lambda: self._download_variant(tts_id, lang_code, variant_id),
    daemon=True,
).start()

4.6 Higher-Order Functions

Functions that take or return other functions:

# Function as argument
def apply_to_segments(segments: list, func):
    """Apply a function to each segment."""
    results = []
    for seg in segments:
        results.append(func(seg))
    return results

# Usage
titles = apply_to_segments(segments, lambda s: s["title"])
lengths = apply_to_segments(segments, lambda s: len(s["text"]))

# Built-in higher-order functions
def is_installed(voice):
    return voice.get("installed", False)

# filter: keep items where function returns True
installed = list(filter(is_installed, all_voices))

# map: transform each item
ids = list(map(lambda v: v["id"], all_voices))

# sorted with key
by_name = sorted(all_voices, key=lambda v: v.get("name", "").lower())

4.8 Recursive Functions

# Factorial (classic example)
def factorial(n: int) -> int:
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

# Recursive directory traversal (used in AIVS)
import os

def find_all_files(directory: str) -> list[str]:
    """Recursively find all files in a directory."""
    result = []
    for entry in os.listdir(directory):
        full_path = os.path.join(directory, entry)
        if os.path.isfile(full_path):
            result.append(full_path)
        elif os.path.isdir(full_path):
            result.extend(find_all_files(full_path))
    return result

4.9 Key Takeaways

  • Use type hints on parameters and return values for clarity
  • Docstrings should explain what, not how
  • Default parameters must be immutable (None for mutable defaults)
  • *args and **kwargs enable flexible function signatures
  • Lambdas are for short, throwaway functions — use def for anything complex
  • Avoid global and nonlocal when possible — they make code harder to reason about
  • Functions should do one thing and do it well (Single Responsibility Principle)

Chapter 5

Strings & Formatting

Learning Objectives

  • Master string methods for manipulation, searching, and transformation

5.1 String Creation Review

# Single and double quotes are equivalent
s1 = 'hello'
s2 = "hello"

# Triple quotes for multi-line strings
text = """This is
a multi-line
string."""

# Escape sequences
s = "Line 1\nLine 2\tTabbed"
s = "She said \"hello\""
s = "Path: C:\\Users\\doc.txt"

# Raw strings (no escape processing)
path = r"C:\Users\doc.txt"        # Backslashes are literal
regex = r"\d+\.\d+"                # Regex patterns

# Bytes vs strings
text = "hello"            # str (Unicode)
data = b"hello"           # bytes (raw bytes)
encoded = text.encode("utf-8")  # str → bytes
decoded = data.decode("utf-8")  # bytes → str

5.2 Essential String Methods

Case Methods

s = "Hello, AI Voice Studio!"
print(s.upper())         # "HELLO, AI VOICE STUDIO!"
print(s.lower())         # "hello, ai voice studio!"
print(s.title())         # "Hello, Ai Voice Studio!"
print(s.capitalize())    # "Hello, ai voice studio!"
print(s.swapcase())      # "hELLO, ai voice studio!"
print(s.casefold())      # Like lower(), but more aggressive

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 2)

  1. Line 1: s = "Hello, AI Voice Studio!"
    Assigns "Hello, AI Voice Studio!" to s.
  2. Line 2: print(s.upper()) # "HELLO, AI VOICE STUDIO!"
    Converts all characters to uppercase. Returns a new string (strings are immutable).
  3. Line 3: print(s.lower()) # "hello, ai voice studio!"
    Converts all characters to lowercase. Returns a new string.
  4. Line 4: print(s.title()) # "Hello, Ai Voice Studio!"
    Capitalizes the first letter of each word.
  5. Line 5: print(s.capitalize()) # "Hello, ai voice studio!"
    Capitalizes the first letter of the string.
  6. Line 6: print(s.swapcase()) # "hELLO, ai voice studio!"
    Swaps case of each character.
  7. Line 7: print(s.casefold()) # Like lower(), but more aggressive
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.

Search and Test Methods

s = "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"

# Finding positions
print(s.find("fox"))        # 16 (index of first occurrence)
print(s.find("fox", 20))    # -1 (not found after index 20)
print(s.rfind("the"))       # 31 (last occurrence)
print(s.count("the"))       # 2

# Boolean tests
print(s.startswith("The"))  # True
print(s.endswith("dog"))    # True
print(s.isalpha())          # False (has spaces)
print("abc123".isalnum())   # True
print("123".isdigit())     # True
print("  \t\n".isspace())  # True

Transformation Methods

# Stripping whitespace
s = "  hello  \n"
print(s.strip())     # "hello"
print(s.lstrip())    # "hello  \n"
print(s.rstrip())    # "  hello"

# Strip specific characters
print("###hello###".strip("#"))  # "hello"

# Replacing
s = "Piper / en_US / medium"
print(s.replace(" / ", "/"))  # "Piper/en_US/medium"

# Splitting and joining
parts = "en_US/medium".split("/")  # ["en_US", "medium"]
joined = " | ".join(parts)          # "en_US | medium"

# Alignment and padding
print(f"'{'hi':10}'")    # 'hi        ' (left-aligned)
print(f"'{'hi':^10}'")   # '    hi    ' (centered)
print(f"'{'hi':>10}'")   # '        hi' (right-aligned)
print(f"'{'hi':*^10}'")  # '****hi****' (fill with *)

:xHex lowercasef"{255:x}"ff
:=+10dSign + paddingf"{42:=+10d}"+ 42

5.6 Strings in TTS Processing (AIVS)

The TTS engine requires careful text preparation before synthesis:

# From documents/splitter.py — text segmentation for TTS
def _split_sentences(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Split text into sentences for TTS processing."""
    import re
    # Split on sentence-ending punctuation
    sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text)
    return [s.strip() for s in sentences if s.strip()]

# From util.py — filename sanitization
def sanitize_filename(name: str, max_length: int = 80) -> str:
    """Remove unsafe characters from filenames."""
    import re
    name = re.sub(r'[<>:"/\\|?*]', '_', name)
    name = re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', name).strip()
    if len(name) > max_length:
        name = name[:max_length].rstrip()
    return name

# From documents/parsers.py — text normalization
def _normalize_text(text: str) -> str:
    """Normalize text for TTS processing."""
    # Remove excessive whitespace
    text = re.sub(r'\n{3,}', '\n\n', text)
    # Normalize Unicode
    text = text.strip()
    return text

# From tts/catalog.py — building voice labels
def _build_voice_label(voice: dict) -> str:
    """Build a display label like 'af_bella (af_bella)'."""
    name = voice.get("name", voice["id"])
    voice_id = voice["id"]
    if name != voice_id:
        return f"{name} ({voice_id})"
    return name

5.7 Unicode and Encoding

# Python 3 strings are Unicode by default
s = "Hello 你好 مرحبا"
print(len(s))  # 14 characters (not bytes)

# Encode to bytes for storage/transmission
encoded = s.encode("utf-8")
print(len(encoded))  # 18 bytes

# Decode back to string
decoded = encoded.decode("utf-8")

# Unicode categories useful for text processing
import unicodedata
for char in "AÍ":
    print(f"{char}: {unicodedata.name(char)}")

5.9 Key Takeaways

  • Strings are immutable — every method returns a new string
  • f-strings are the preferred formatting method (concise, readable, fast)
  • str methods cover virtually all text processing needs
  • str.split() and str.join() are your best friends for text manipulation
  • Unicode is built-in — Python 3 handles international text natively
  • The AIVS project uses string processing for text normalization, filename sanitization, and voice label formatting

6.1 Lists — Ordered, Mutable Sequences

# Creating lists
engines = ["Piper", "Kokoro", "Matcha", "Kitten"]
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
mixed = [42, "hello", True, None]  # Any types
empty = []

# Accessing elements (0-based indexing)
print(engines[0])      # "Piper"
print(engines[-1])     # "Kitten" (last element)

# Slicing (returns a new list)
print(engines[1:3])    # ["Kokoro", "Matcha"]
print(engines[::2])     # ["Piper", "Matcha"] (every other)
print(engines[::-1])    # Reversed copy

# Modifying
engines[0] = "Piper v2"
engines.append("XTTS")
engines.insert(1, "New Engine")
engines.extend(["OmniVoice", "Server"])
engines.remove("Matcha")
popped = engines.pop()    # Remove and return last
popped = engines.pop(0)  # Remove and return first
del engines[0]          # Delete by index

# Useful operations
print(len(engines))         # Count
print("Piper" in engines)   # Membership test: True
engines.sort()                # Sort in-place (alphabetical)
engines.sort(reverse=True)   # Reverse sort
engines.reverse()             # Reverse in-place

# Count and index
engines = ["Piper", "Kokoro", "Piper"]
print(engines.count("Piper"))  # 2
print(engines.index("Kokoro")) # 1

# Copying (important!)
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a.copy()     # Independent copy
b = a[:]          # Also an independent copy
b = list(a)       # Also an independent copy
# b = a          # WRONG: just another reference to same list!

6.2 Tuples — Ordered, Immutable Sequences

# Creating tuples
point = (3, 4)
single = (42,)       # Trailing comma required for single-element tuple
empty = ()
# Parentheses are optional for packing
point = 3, 4          # Also a tuple

# Accessing (same as lists)
print(point[0])       # 3

# Cannot modify!
# point[0] = 5  # TypeError: 'tuple' does not support item assignment

# Named tuples — readable tuples with field names
from collections import namedtuple

Segment = namedtuple("Segment", ["index", "title", "text"])
seg = Segment(index=1, title="Chapter 1", text="Once upon...")
print(seg.index)     # 1 (named access)
print(seg[0])        # 1 (also indexable)

# Unpacking
index, title, text = seg

6.3 Dictionaries — Key-Value Mapping

# Creating dicts
voice = {
    "id": "af_bella",
    "name": "Bella",
    "sid": 2,
    "language": "en",
}

# Accessing
print(voice["id"])           # "af_bella"
print(voice.get("speed", 1.0))  # 1.0 (default if key missing)
print(voice.get("speed"))      # None (no default)

# Modifying
voice["sample_rate"] = 24000   # Add/update
del voice["sid"]              # Delete
removed = voice.pop("language") # Remove and return

# Iteration
for key in voice:              # Keys (default)
    print(key)

for key, value in voice.items():  # Key-value pairs
    print(f"{key}: {value}")

for value in voice.values():   # Values only
    print(value)

# Merging
defaults = {"rate": 1.0, "pitch": 1.0}
overrides = {"rate": 1.5, "volume": 0.8}

# Python 3.9+ merge operator
merged = defaults | overrides   # {"rate": 1.5, "pitch": 1.0, "volume": 0.8}

# Classic merge
merged = {**defaults, **overrides}

# setdefault — get or set in one step
config = {}
config.setdefault("threads", 4)  # Sets and returns 4
config.setdefault("threads", 8)  # Returns existing 4

Dictionaries in AIVS Settings

# From ai_voice_studio/settings.py
class Settings:
    def __init__(self):
        self._data: dict = {
            "theme": "system",
            "audio_mode": "page_with_h1",
            "recording.rate": 1.0,
            "recording.pitch": 1.0,
            "recording.volume": 1.0,
            "recording.output_format": "wav",
            "developer_mode": False,
        }

    def get(self, key: str, default=None):
        """Dot-notation get: settings.get('recording.rate')"""
        keys = key.split(".")
        obj = self._data
        for k in keys:
            if isinstance(obj, dict):
                obj = obj.get(k)
                if obj is None:
                    return default
            else:
                return default
        return obj

    def set(self, key: str, value):
        """Dot-notation set: settings.set('recording.rate', 1.5)"""
        keys = key.split(".")
        obj = self._data
        for k in keys[:-1]:
            obj = obj.setdefault(k, {})
        obj[keys[-1]] = value

6.4 Sets — Unordered, Unique Elements

# Creating sets
languages = {"en", "zh", "ja", "ko"}
empty_set = set()  # {} creates an empty dict, not set!

# From a list (removes duplicates)
voices = ["af", "am", "af", "bf", "am"]
unique_voices = set(voices)  # {"af", "am", "bf"}

# Set operations
a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5, 6}

print(a | b)     # Union: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
print(a & b)     # Intersection: {3, 4}
print(a - b)     # Difference: {1, 2}
print(a ^ b)     # Symmetric difference: {1, 2, 5, 6}

# Membership (very fast — O(1) lookup)
print(3 in a)    # True

# Frozenset — immutable set (can be dict key)
frozen = frozenset([1, 2, 3])

6.5 Choosing the Right Collection

NeedUseWhy
Ordered sequence, mutablelistIndex access, append, sort
Ordered sequence, immutabletupleHashable, slightly faster
Key-value mappingdictO(1) lookup by key
Unique elements, fast membershipsetO(1) in test
Record with named fieldsnamedtupleReadable, immutable
Fixed-structure record@dataclassMutable, type-hinted (Ch 10)

6.7 Useful Collection Functions

# sorted() — returns a new sorted list
voices = ["bf", "af", "am"]
sorted_voices = sorted(voices)                    # ["af", "am", "bf"]
sorted_voices = sorted(voices, reverse=True)       # ["bf", "am", "af"]
sorted_voices = sorted(voices, key=len)            # ["af", "am", "bf"]

# sorted with dict key
voices_sorted = sorted(voice_list, key=lambda v: v.get("name", ""))

# min, max, sum
sids = [v["sid"] for v in voices]
print(min(sids), max(sids), sum(sids))

# any() and all()
has_gpu = any(detected.values())       # True if any value is True
all_ok = all(status.values())          # True if all values are True

# zip() — iterate multiple sequences in parallel
names = ["Piper", "Kokoro"]
counts = [153, 103]
for name, count in zip(names, counts):
    print(f"{name}: {count} voices")

# reversed() — returns an iterator
for v in reversed([1, 2, 3]):
    print(v)  # 3, 2, 1

# enumerate() with custom start
for i, voice in enumerate(voices, start=1):
    print(f"Voice #{i}: {voice}")

6.8 collections Module

from collections import Counter, defaultdict, deque, OrderedDict

# Counter — count occurrences
text = "hello world hello python hello"
word_counts = Counter(text.split())
print(word_counts)          # Counter({'hello': 3, 'world': 1, ...})
print(word_counts.most_common(2))  # [('hello', 3), ('world', 1)]

# defaultdict — dict with default values
voices_by_tts = defaultdict(list)
for v in all_voices:
    voices_by_tts[v["tts"]].append(v)  # No KeyError if key missing

# deque — double-ended queue (fast insert/delete at both ends)
history = deque(maxlen=10)  # Auto-removes oldest
history.append("action1")
history.appendleft("action0")

6.9 Key Takeaways

  • Lists for ordered, mutable sequences (most common)
  • Tuples for fixed records and dict keys
  • Dicts for key-value data (the backbone of AIVS settings and catalog)
  • Sets for unique elements and fast membership testing
  • Copy correctly — b = a creates a reference, not a copy
  • Dict.get() with a default avoids KeyError
  • The AIVS catalog is a deeply nested dict structure: TTS → language → variant → voice
Exercise 6.1: Given a list of voice dictionaries, write a dict comprehension that groups them by language code. Result: {"en": [...], "zh": [...], ...}
Exercise 6.2: Implement a simple LRUCache class using OrderedDict with a maxlen parameter.

Chapter 7

File I/O

Learning Objectives

  • Read and write text and binary files
  • Understand file modes, encoding, and context managers
  • Use the pathlib module for modern path handling
  • See how AIVS reads/writes JSON settings and project files

7.1 Opening and Closing Files

# The "classic" way (don't do this in modern Python)
f = open("data.txt", "r")
content = f.read()
f.close()  # Must close manually!

# The correct way — context manager (auto-closes)
with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    content = f.read()
# f is automatically closed here, even if an exception occurs

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 1)

  1. Line 1: # The "classic" way (don't do this in modern Python)
    A comment: The "classic" way (don't do this in modern Python).
  2. Line 2: f = open("data.txt", "r")
    Opens a file and returns a file object. Supports modes: 'r' (read), 'w' (write), 'a' (append), 'b' (binary).
  3. Line 3: content = f.read()
    Reads the entire file contents as a string.
  4. Line 4: f.close() # Must close manually!
    Closes the file and flushes the write buffer. Prefer using 'with' instead.
  5. Line 5: # The correct way — context manager (auto-closes)
    A comment: The correct way — context manager (auto-closes).
  6. Line 6: with open("data.txt", "r") as f:
    Opens a file using a context manager. The file is automatically closed when the block exits, even if an error occurs.
  7. Line 7: content = f.read()
    Reads the entire file contents as a string.
  8. Line 8: # f is automatically closed here, even if an exception occurs
    A comment: f is automatically closed here, even if an exception occurs.

File Modes

ModeDescription
"r"Read (default). File must exist.
"w"Write. Creates or truncates file.
"a"Append. Creates if doesn't exist.
"x"Exclusive create. Fails if file exists.
"r+"Read + write. File must exist.
"rb"Read binary.
"wb"Write binary.

# Read as bytes (for binary files like audio)

    data = f.read()  # Returns bytes object

AIVS Settings Pattern

# From ai_voice_studio/settings.py
def load(self) -> None:
    """Load settings from disk, merging with defaults."""
    if os.path.isfile(self._path):
        with open(self._path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            stored = json.load(f)
        # Merge: defaults + stored values
        self._data = {**self._defaults, **stored}

def save(self) -> None:
    """Save current settings to disk."""
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(self._path), exist_ok=True)
    with open(self._path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(self._data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)

7.8 File I/O in AIVS

# From project.py — atomic JSON write
def save_project(project_dir: str, data: dict) -> None:
    """Save project.json atomically (write to temp, then rename)."""
    import tempfile
    path = os.path.join(project_dir, "project.json")
    # Write to a temp file first (atomic on same filesystem)
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=project_dir, suffix=".tmp")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
        # Atomic rename (on same filesystem)
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except:
        os.unlink(tmp)
        raise

# From tts/downloader.py — streaming download with progress
def _download_file(url: str, dest: str, progress=None) -> None:
    """Download a file with progress reporting."""
    import requests
    with requests.get(url, stream=True) as resp:
        total = int(resp.headers.get("content-length", 0))
        downloaded = 0
        with open(dest, "wb") as f:
            for chunk in resp.iter_content(chunk_size=8192):
                f.write(chunk)
                downloaded += len(chunk)
                if progress:
                    progress(downloaded, total)

7.9 Temporary Files

import tempfile

# Temporary file (auto-deleted when closed)
with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".wav", delete=True) as tmp:
    tmp.write(audio_data)
    tmp.flush()
    # Process the file...
# File is deleted automatically

# Temporary directory
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
    # Work with tmpdir...
    pass
# Directory and all contents deleted automatically

7.10 Key Takeaways

  • Always use with statements for file I/O (context managers auto-close)
  • Always specify encoding="utf-8" for text files
  • JSON is the standard format for settings and project data in AIVS
  • Atomic writes (write to temp file, then rename) prevent corruption
  • pathlib is the modern way to handle file paths
  • For streaming large files, read in chunks to avoid loading everything into memory

8.2 try / except / else / finally

try:
    # Code that might fail
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    # Handle the specific error
    print("Cannot divide by zero")
else:
    # Runs only if NO exception occurred
    print(f"Result: {result}")
finally:
    # ALWAYS runs, whether or not an exception occurred
    print("Cleanup")

# Catching multiple exception types
try:
    load_voice_model(path)
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("Model not found — download it first")
except PermissionError:
    print("Permission denied")
except OSError as exc:
    print(f"OS error: {exc}")

# Catching multiple types in one handler
try:
    download_model(url)
except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as exc:
    print(f"Network error: {exc}")

# Catching everything (use sparingly!)
try:
    risky_operation()
except Exception:
    print("Something went wrong")
    # ⚠️ Don't catch BaseException — it kills Ctrl+C!

8.5 Exception Handling Patterns in AIVS

# Pattern 1: Graceful degradation with logging
try:
    result = load_model(path)
except FileNotFoundError:
    log.warning("Model not found at {path}")
    result = None
except Exception as exc:
    log.error("Failed to load model: {exc}", exc_info=True)
    result = None

# Pattern 2: Retry with fallback
def download_with_fallback(urls):
    """Try multiple URLs until one works."""
    for url in urls:
        try:
            return download(url)
        except DownloadError as exc:
            log.warning("Failed {url}: {exc}")
    raise DownloadError("All download sources failed")

# Pattern 3: Suppressing expected exceptions
import contextlib
with contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError):
    os.unlink(temp_file)  # Ignore if already deleted

# Pattern 4: Safe operations in GUI callbacks
def _on_download(self, _):
    try:
        self._start_download()
    except Exception as exc:
        # Never let exceptions crash the GUI!
        wx.MessageBox(
            f"Download failed: {exc}",
            "Error",
            style=wx.OK | wx.ICON_ERROR,
        )

# Pattern 5: noqa comments for intentional bare exceptions
try:
    some_risky_call()
except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001
    pass  # Intentionally ignore all errors

8.7 Exception Best Practices

Rules for Exception Handling:
  1. Be specific — catch FileNotFoundError, not Exception
  2. Don't swallow errors silently — at least log them
  3. Never use bare except: — always specify except Exception:
  4. Use custom exceptions to distinguish application errors from library errors
  5. In GUI code, always catch exceptions to prevent crashes
  6. In worker threads, catch and report exceptions via events

8.8 Key Takeaways

  • try/except/else/finally is the full error handling pattern
  • Catch specific exceptions — never use bare except:
  • Custom exceptions make application errors distinguishable from system errors
  • Always log exceptions with exc_info=True for debugging
  • In AIVS, exceptions are caught at GUI boundaries and worker threads

9.1 Import Basics

# Import the entire module
import os
import json
print(os.path.join("a", "b"))

# Import with alias
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])

# Import specific names
from os.path import join, exists
print(join("a", "b"))

# Import everything (don't do this!)
from os import *  # Pollutes namespace

# Conditional import
if sys.platform == "win32":
    import winsound

9.2 Creating Modules

Any .py file is a module. If you create mymodule.py:

# mymodule.py
"""My custom module for audio utilities."""

SAMPLE_RATE = 24000

def format_duration(seconds: float) -> str:
    """Format seconds as HH:MM:SS."""
    h = int(seconds // 3600)
    m = int((seconds % 3600) // 60)
    s = int(seconds % 60)
    return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}"

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 2)

  1. Line 1: # mymodule.py
    A comment: mymodule.py.
  2. Line 2: """My custom module for audio utilities."""
    Docstring: My custom module for audio utilities.. Documents the purpose of the following code.
  3. Line 3: SAMPLE_RATE = 24000
    Assigns 24000 to SAMPLE_RATE.
  4. Line 4: def format_duration(seconds: float) -> str:
    Defines function format_duration accepting (seconds), returning str.
  5. Line 5: """Format seconds as HH:MM:SS."""
    Docstring: Format seconds as HH:MM:SS.. Documents the purpose of the following code.
  6. Line 6: h = int(seconds // 3600)
    Converts a value to an integer. Truncates floats toward zero. Raises ValueError for invalid strings.
  7. Line 7: m = int((seconds % 3600) // 60)
    Converts a value to an integer. Truncates floats toward zero. Raises ValueError for invalid strings.
  8. Line 8: s = int(seconds % 60)
    Converts a value to an integer. Truncates floats toward zero. Raises ValueError for invalid strings.
  9. Line 9: return f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}"
    Returns f"{h:02d}:{m:02d}:{s:02d}" to the caller.

Then in another file:

print(mymodule.format_duration(3661))  # "01:01:01"

9.3 Creating Packages

A package is a directory of modules with an __init__.py:

ai_voice_studio/           # Package directory

9.4 Absolute vs. Relative Imports

# Absolute imports (preferred — clearer)
from ai_voice_studio.paths import user_data_dir
from ai_voice_studio.tts.catalog import get_tts_list
from ai_voice_studio.settings import Settings

# Relative imports (within the same package)
from . import paths            # Same package
from .. import settings         # Parent package
from .tts import catalog        # Sibling package
from ..paths import user_data_dir # Parent's module
from .models import ModelStore   # Same package's module

# In AIVS, relative imports are used within the package:
# From tts/engine.py:
from .. import paths
from ..settings import Settings

9.5 The __name__ and __main__ Pattern

# Every module has a __name__ variable
# When imported: __name__ == "mymodule"
# When run directly: __name__ == "__main__"

def main():
    print("Running my module!")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()  # Only runs when executed directly

Explain Line by Line Code Description (Block 7)

  1. Line 1: # Every module has a __name__ variable
    A comment: Every module has a __name__ variable.
  2. Line 2: # When imported: __name__ == "mymodule"
    A comment: When imported: __name__ == "mymodule".
  3. Line 3: # When run directly: __name__ == "__main__"
    A comment: When run directly: __name__ == "__main__".
  4. Line 4: def main():
    Defines function main.
  5. Line 5: print("Running my module!")
    Outputs text to the console. The primary way to display information during development and debugging.
  6. Line 6: if __name__ == "__main__":
    Checks condition: __name__ == "__main__". The indented block runs only when this is True.
  7. Line 7: main() # Only runs when executed directly
    Calls function main().

This pattern is used throughout AIVS:

# main.py — the application entry point
def main() -> int:
    app = wx.App(False)
    frame = MainFrame(None)
    frame.Show()
    return app.MainLoop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# ai_voice_studio/clone/worker.py — subprocess entry point
def main() -> int:
    # Worker loop reading JSON commands from stdin
    for line in sys.stdin:
        ...
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

9.6 Import Hooks and Dynamic Imports

# Importlib — dynamic imports at runtime
import importlib
module = importlib.import_module("ai_voice_studio.tts.catalog")

# Used in the addon system
import importlib.util
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(
    "_addon_my_tts",
    "/path/to/addon/__init__.py",
)
module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
sys.modules["_addon_my_tts"] = module
spec.loader.exec_module(module)

# Lazy imports (import only when needed)
def heavy_function():
    import numpy  # Only imported when function is called
    return np.array([1, 2, 3])

9.7 Standard Library Highlights

ModulePurposeAIVS Usage
osOS interface, paths, environmentFile operations, paths
jsonJSON parsing and writingSettings, project files
loggingLogging frameworkDebug and info logging
threadingThread-based parallelismBackground TTS synthesis
subprocessProcess managementFFmpeg, pip, worker processes
reRegular expressionsText processing, parsing
pathlibObject-oriented pathsModern path handling
tempfileTemporary files and dirsAtomic writes, pip installs
zipfileZIP archive handlingDAISY book export
uuidUnique identifiersDAISY book UIDs

9.8 Key Takeaways

  • Any .py file is a module; a directory with __init__.py is a package
  • Use absolute imports for clarity (from ai_voice_studio.paths import ...)
  • Relative imports are for within-package references only
  • The if __name__ == "__main__" pattern allows files to be both imported and run
  • Dynamic imports via importlib enable the AIVS addon system
  • Lazy imports (inside functions) improve startup time for heavy dependencies

Object-Oriented Programming Basics

Learning Objectives

  • Understand classes, objects, and the __init__ method

10.1 Classes and Objects

class TtsVoice:
    """Represents a single TTS voice."""

    # Class attribute (shared by all instances)
    sample_rate = 24000

    def __init__(self, voice_id: str, name: str, sid: int = 0):
        """Initialize a new TtsVoice instance."""
        # Instance attributes (unique to each object)
        self.voice_id = voice_id
        self.name = name
        self.sid = sid
        self.is_loaded = False

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        """Developer-friendly string representation."""
        return f"TtsVoice({self.voice_id!r}, {self.name!r}, sid={self.sid})"

    def load(self):
        """Load the voice model."""
        print(f"Loading {self.name} (sid={self.sid})...")
        self.is_loaded = True

    def synthesize(self, text: str) -> "np.ndarray":
        """Synthesize text using this voice."""
        if not self.is_loaded:
            self.load()
        print(f"Synthesizing '{text[:30]}' with {self.name}")
        # ... actual synthesis logic

# Creating objects (instances)
bella = TtsVoice("af_bella", "Bella", sid=2)
adam = TtsVoice("am_adam", "Adam", sid=1)

# Using objects
bella.load()
bella.synthesize("Hello world")

# Class attribute shared by all instances
print(TtsVoice.sample_rate)      # 24000
print(bella.sample_rate)         # 24000 (same)

# Check type
print(isinstance(bella, TtsVoice))  # True

10.2 The __init__ Method

__init__ is the constructor — it runs when you create a new object:

class Settings:
    def __init__(self, path: str | None = None):
        """Initialize settings with optional file path."""
        self._path = path
        self._data: dict = {}
        self._load()

    def _load(self):
        """Load settings from disk."""
        if self._path and os.path.isfile(self._path):
            with open(self._path, "r") as f:
                self._data = json.load(f)

# __init__ parameters have default values
s1 = Settings()                    # No path
s2 = Settings("/path/to/settings.json")  # With path

10.3 Instance vs. Class Attributes

class Engine:
    # Class attributes — shared by ALL instances
    version = "1.0"
    _cache = {}  # Shared cache

    def __init__(self, engine_id: str):
        # Instance attributes — unique per instance
        self.engine_id = engine_id
        self.is_ready = False

e1 = Engine("piper")
e2 = Engine("kokoro")

# Instance attributes differ
print(e1.engine_id)  # "piper"
print(e2.engine_id)  # "kokoro"

# Class attributes are shared
print(e1.version)    # "1.0"
print(e2.version)    # "1.0"

# Modifying a class attribute on an instance creates an instance attribute
e1.version = "2.0"   # Only e1 is affected
print(e1.version)    # "2.0"
print(e2.version)    # "1.0" (still uses class attribute)
print(Engine.version) # "1.0" (class attribute unchanged)

10.4 Types of Methods

class AudioFile:
    # Class attribute
    MAX_SIZE_MB = 100

    def __init__(self, path: str, data: bytes):
        self.path = path
        self.data = data

    # Instance method — accesses 'self'
    def size_mb(self) -> float:
        return len(self.data) / (1024 * 1024)

    # Class method — accesses 'cls' (the class itself)
    @classmethod
    def from_file(cls, path: str) -> "AudioFile":
        """Alternative constructor from a file path."""
        with open(path, "rb") as f:
            data = f.read()
        return cls(path, data)  # cls() = AudioFile()

    # Static method — no access to self or cls
    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_format(path: str) -> bool:
        """Check if file extension is supported."""
        return path.lower().endswith((".wav", ".mp3", ".flac"))

# Using all three types
f1 = AudioFile("output.wav", audio_bytes)    # Regular constructor
f2 = AudioFile.from_file("output.wav")       # Class method constructor
print(f1.size_mb())                            # Instance method
print(AudioFile.is_valid_format("test.wav"))  # Static method

  5. Line 5: self.path = path

  6. Line 6: self.data = data

  9. Line 9: return len(self.data) / (1024 * 1024)
    Returns the number of items in a sequence (string, list, dict, tuple). Essential for loop bounds and validation.
  10. Line 10: # Class method — accesses 'cls' (the class itself)
    A comment: Class method — accesses 'cls' (the class itself).
  11. Line 11: @classmethod
    Decorator that receives the class (cls) as the first argument instead of the instance.
  12. Line 12: def from_file(cls, path: str) -> "AudioFile":

10.5 Special (Dunder) Methods

class Segment:
    def __init__(self, index: int, title: str, text: str):
        self.index = index
        self.title = title
        self.text = text

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        """Developer string: Segment(1, 'Chapter 1')"""
        return f"Segment({self.index}, {self.title!r})"

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        """User-facing string: "Chapter 1" """
        return self.title

    def __eq__(self, other) -> bool:
        """Equality comparison."""
        if not isinstance(other, Segment):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.index == other.index

    def __lt__(self, other) -> bool:
        """Less-than comparison (enables sorting)."""
        return self.index < other.index

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        """len(segment) returns text length."""
        return len(self.text)

    def __bool__(self) -> bool:
        """bool(segment) is True if text is non-empty."""
        return bool(self.text.strip())

# Usage
seg = Segment(1, "Chapter 1", "Once upon a time...")
print(repr(seg))  # Segment(1, 'Chapter 1')
print(str(seg))   # Chapter 1
print(len(seg))   # 22

segments = [seg2, seg1]
sorted_segs = sorted(segments)  # Works because of __lt__

10.6 Properties

class VoiceEntry:
    def __init__(self, voice_id: str, sid: int):
        self._voice_id = voice_id
        self._sid = sid

    @property
    def voice_id(self) -> str:
        """Read-only property."""
        return self._voice_id

    @property
    def display_name(self) -> str:
        """Computed property — not stored, calculated on access."""
        return f"{self._voice_id} (sid={self._sid})"

    @property
    def sid(self) -> int:
        return self._sid

    @sid.setter
    def sid(self, value: int):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("SID must be non-negative")
        self._sid = value

v = VoiceEntry("af_bella", 2)
print(v.display_name)  # "af_bella (sid=2)" — computed, not stored
v.sid = 5              # Uses setter with validation

        """Return list of all installed voice entries."""
        ...

# From clone/__init__.py — CloneClient manages a subprocess
class CloneClient:
    def __init__(self, timeout: float = 600.0):
        self._proc: subprocess.Popen | None = None
        self._lock = threading.RLock()
        self._timeout = timeout
        self._next_id = 0

    def _ensure_proc(self):
        """Start the worker subprocess if not running."""
        if self._proc is not None and self._proc.poll() is None:
            return  # Already running
        # Start new subprocess...

    def synthesize(self, text, sample_wav, language="en", speed=1.0):
        """Synthesize text using the worker subprocess."""
        self._ensure_proc()
        resp = self._request({"cmd": "synthesize", "text": text, ...})
        return np.frombuffer(base64.b64decode(resp["wav"]), dtype=np.int16)

    def close(self):
        """Shut down the worker subprocess."""
        with self._lock:
            if self._proc:
                self._proc.stdin.write(json.dumps({"cmd": "quit"}) + "\n")
                self._proc.terminate()
